one_liner: Lossy PNG palette quantizer (CLI plus libimagequant library); author claims its fast setting is 2.5-6x ImageMagick's quantizer.
what_it_does: pngquant converts 24/32-bit RGBA PNGs to 8-bit palette PNGs with an alpha channel, picking the fewest colours that meet a JPEG-like --quality min-max target and skipping files that cannot reach the minimum (exit code 99). The engine, libimagequant, works on raw RGBA buffers only (bring your own decoder and encoder): liq_attr_create, liq_set_speed/quality/max_colors, liq_image_create_rgba, liq_image_quantize, liq_write_remapped_image, or the imagequant Rust crate (Attributes::new, quantize, remapped). It is not a drop-in for ImageMagick: there is no -colors flag set, no file formats besides PNG in the CLI, and you get a palette plus 1-byte indices back.
how_it_is_fast: A histogram of 32-bit colours goes into a hash map (posterized to fewer bits at speeds 8-10 or past a million colours), then a variance-driven modified median cut builds the palette, refined by weighted k-means (Voronoi) iterations in a feedback loop. Nearest-colour search uses a vantage-point tree with a 'likely index' shortcut and a half-distance-to-nearest-neighbour early exit. The colour distance (premultiplied alpha, max of over-black and over-white error) is a 4-lane SSE, NEON or WASM simd128 routine. The speed knob trades work directly: speed 4 (default) runs 12 k-means iterations and 20 feedback trials over up to 1.7M histogram entries, speed 10 runs no k-means, no feedback loop, no dither or contrast maps and caps the histogram at 131,072 entries; k-means, remap and dithering run on rayon threads.
when_to_use: Shrinking PNG assets for the web or apps where 8-bit palette plus full alpha is acceptable (README: often 60-80% smaller than 24/32-bit PNG).
Real-time palette generation (map tiles, GIF frames) with --speed 10/11 or liq_set_speed(10), where the author says quality drops about 5% for about 8x the speed of the default.
Batch pipelines that need a quality gate: --quality min-max plus --skip-if-larger rejects images that would degrade too much.
C or Rust code that needs a palette quantizer with alpha-aware dithering, fixed palette colours, importance maps or remapping onto a background (GIF animation).
GPL-3.0-or-later projects, or closed-source ones willing to buy the commercial licence.
when_not_to_use: Permissive-licence products that cannot take GPL-3.0-or-later and will not pay for the commercial licence.
Pure C/C++ toolchains that cannot add Rust: since libimagequant 4 / pngquant 3 the engine is Rust (C ABI kept), so building needs cargo; the C99 code lives only on the unmaintained 2.x branch.

Pipelines that need bit-identical output across machines: open libimagequant issue #130 shows palettes of 111 vs 120 colours for the same image on x86_64 and aarch64 at speeds 1-7, and dithered remapping splits large images into chunks by core count (see gotchas).

When you need a quality or speed comparison against ImageMagick, Pillow or libvips you can trust: none is published in either repo, and open issue #424 reports desaturated colours from pngquant --nofs where ImageMagick's PNG8 output looked right.
Images that must keep more than 256 colours, or 16-bit precision: output is 8-bit palette (the large_palettes feature goes to 2048 colours but not for remapping).

integration.form: CLI binary (Rust main plus C rwpng.c/pngquant.c via the cc crate); library as Rust crate imagequant or static lib libimagequant_sys.a with libimagequant.h (cargo-c for a shared lib)
integration.dependencies: CLI: libpng (libpng-sys), zlib, optional Little CMS 2 (default feature) or Cocoa on macOS, getopts, rayon via imagequant. Library: arrayvec, rgb, rayon and thread_local (threads feature); no runtime deps for C users of the static lib.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.67 for pngquant 3.0.4 (Cargo.toml rust-version; libimagequant says 1.65 in Cargo.toml and 1.70+ in its README), plus a C99 compiler for the CLI's C files
integration.platforms: Any Rust target; SIMD colour distance on x86_64 (SSE), aarch64 (NEON) and wasm32 (simd128), scalar elsewhere; threads must be disabled for WASM; no_std build available without threads
integration.thread_safety: Documented: separate liq_attr/liq_result objects can run in parallel threads; one object may move between threads but not be used concurrently. Internally multi-threaded via rayon (RAYON_NUM_THREADS), disable with --no-default-features.

gotchas: Stale docs: the pngquant README still says C99, OpenMP and SSE, and pngquant.1 says the default speed is 3; the code (pngquant.c help, imagequant set_speed) uses 4, threading is rayon, and libimagequant's README says OpenMP 'has been dropped entirely'. The C file's version string still reads '(January 2022)'.
Speed 11 exists only in the CLI: it maps to library speed 10 plus --nofs and fast PNG compression; liq_set_speed accepts 1-10.

Dithered output depends on the machine: remap_to_palette_floyd splits images over about 1 MP into up to num_cpus() chunks (std::thread::available_parallelism, not RAYON_NUM_THREADS), and each chunk restarts error diffusion after two warm-up rows, so results can differ between machines with different core counts.
The palette is refined during remapping (one more k-means pass), so read the palette after remap_into, not before; quality numbers can be -1 at high speeds unless a quality range is set.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling is a palette quantizer: the siblings resize, convert colour spaces or manage ICC profiles. Pillow can call libimagequant itself (its quantize method has a libimagequant option when Pillow is built against it), so use pngquant/libimagequant directly when you want the quality gate, the speed knob and alpha-aware dithering, and Pillow's own fast-octree mode only when speed matters more than colour fidelity.
verified_claims_summary: The only comparison with the baseline is first-party and snippet-only: a 'fast and rough' libimagequant setting said to be 2.5 to 6 times faster than ImageMagick's then-current quantizer 'while still mostly winning in quality', from the author's proposal thread on the legacy ImageMagick forum (blocked; no images, versions, settings, compiler or hardware). The repo's own figure, speed 10 being about 8x faster than the default at about 5% lower quality, is a self-comparison, and the repo's bench file (benches/bench.rs) times only libimagequant on a private image (/Users/kornel/Desktop/canvas.png) with no baseline.
status_note: Active (pngquant last commit 2026-06-21, libimagequant 4.5.0 with commits on 2026-06-21 and a WASM SIMD path added 2026-02-11), dual-licensed GPL-3.0-or-later or commercial, so copyable under copyleft; the C 2.x branch is the only all-C option and is not maintained.
measurement_notes: No correctness bug behind the catalogued number was found, and no new number could be checked: the ImageMagick ratio is still snippet-only and first-party (C stays right). Things the orchestrator may want as caveats: (1) the claim compares a fast-and-rough setting (speed 10 maps to 0 k-means iterations, 0 feedback-loop trials, no dither or contrast maps, 1-bit posterization, histogram capped at 131,072 entries in imagequant attr.rs) with ImageMagick's default quantizer, so it is not equal work. (2) The engine measured in the old thread was the C libimagequant 2.x; today's engine is the Rust rewrite, so the old ratio may not describe current code in either direction. (3) The only bench in the repos (libimagequant benches/bench.rs) has no baseline and reads a private file. (4) Output is not deterministic across machines: libimagequant issue #130 (opened 2026-10-01, pngquant 3.0.3, speeds 1-7) and core-count-dependent dither chunking in remap.rs. (5) A WebSearch hit, github.com/Chadys/QuantizeImageMethods, times Pillow's median cut (2.68 s), maximum coverage (1.93 s) and fast octree (0.47 s) for 10 iterations on its image set but does not time libimagequant, so it gives no ratio for this entry.
